title: Headline income and official poverty improved while supplemental poverty and full-year insurance coverage stayed broadly flat
source_unit: U.S. Census Bureau CPS ASEC 2025 income, poverty, and health-insurance estimates released September 15, 2026

denominator.unit: U.S. population and households represented by the 2026 CPS Annual Social and Economic Supplement; no single pooled respondent denominator is reported in the release

real_median_household_income.value: $87,460 in 2025, up 2.6% from $85,210 in 2024 and the highest recorded level in the series dating to 1967

official_poverty.value: Official poverty fell 0.5 percentage points to 10.2%, or 34.5 million people; the child poverty rate fell to a historic low of 13.4%
official_poverty.unit: percent and people in official poverty

supplemental_poverty.value: Supplemental Poverty Measure was 13.1% in 2025, not statistically different from 2024
supplemental_poverty.unit: percent of U.S. population under the SPM

health_insurance.value: 26.7 million people, or 7.9%, were uninsured for the entire year, not statistically different from 2024; public coverage was 35.8%, also not statistically different
health_insurance.unit: percent and people without full-year insurance or with public coverage

coverage_route_shift.value: Public coverage for adults ages 19-64 declined 0.5 percentage points to 17.3%, driven by a 0.6-point Medicaid decline; employment-based insurance covered 53.5% of the population for some or all of the year

distribution_context.value: Income at the 90th percentile rose 1.7%, while income at the 10th percentile did not change significantly; the Gini index was not significantly different

observations.method: Census Bureau national estimates from the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement, with separate pretax money-income, official-poverty, Supplemental Poverty Measure, and health-insurance concepts.
observations.uncertainty: The measures use different resource concepts and universes: official poverty excludes many transfers, while the SPM includes taxes, transfers, work and medical expenses, and geographic housing costs. Year-to-year comparisons are subject to sampling and nonsampling error, population controls, and the release's stated statistical-significance tests.
observations.subgroup: U.S. households and individuals overall, with reported contrasts by age, race and ethnicity, earnings, and insurance route; this record retains the national divergence rather than making subgroup causal claims.
observations.counterinterpretation: A record median income and lower official poverty can reflect real improvement without eliminating material strain captured by the SPM, health costs, housing costs, or coverage transitions. Flat national insurance coverage does not mean stable access for every age, state, or income group.

related_sources.claim: Official health-insurance report provides the coverage definitions and 2025 estimates.

boundary: This record adds a realized household-material and coverage layer. It does not infer household wellbeing from median income alone, estimate causal policy effects, resolve state or subgroup heterogeneity, or treat official poverty and the SPM as interchangeable measures.
